name: Industrious Labs (Giving Green, 2022 CEA)
summary: Campaigns for cleaner heavy industry (aluminium, steel, cement) in North America. Giving Green's 2022 estimate of what its campaign to get a major automaker to buy low-carbon aluminium costs per tonne of CO₂e, rebuilt from the figures in Giving Green's deep dive.

source.title: Industrious Labs: Top Climate Nonprofit Evaluation (deep dive, updated November 2024; cost-effectiveness analysis from 2022)

resources.title: Giving Green, Industrious Labs: Top Climate Nonprofit Evaluation
resources.note: The web page says only that Industrious Labs is "highly cost-effective"; the figures are in the downloadable deep dive. Giving Green's spreadsheet isn't published, so the model is built from the figures stated in the deep dive's text, each quoted on its row. Giving Green did not update the 2022 analysis in 2024.

sections.title: The aluminium campaign
sections.explainer: Giving Green modelled one campaign: getting a major global automaker to commit to low-carbon aluminium for its US production, then the knock-on effects on its global production, on the rest of the car industry, and on half the global aluminium industry. For each step it guessed how much Industrious Labs raises the chance of the commitment and how many years sooner it comes; low-carbon aluminium is taken to cut emissions by about 80%. Giving Green states the result at three widths of effect, which this model turns into tonnes.

sections.title: From cost per tonne to tonnes per dollar
sections.explainer: charityevals' step after Giving Green's bottom line: Giving Green reports dollars per tonne; the site needs tonnes per dollar, and how much air pollution those tonnes cut. Most of primary aluminium's emissions come from the electricity smelters use, much of it coal power, so a good share of these tonnes is coal not burned (docs/normalization.md 2.5). The tonnes come years after the money is spent, so they are discounted for that wait at the site's discount rate.

sections.title: Staff pay below market
sections.explainer: charityevals' step, not the evaluator's: with credit by share of resources on, staff's pay below what they could earn elsewhere counts as an in-kind contribution and gets its share of the outcome. Off by default.

source.title: Giving Green, Industrious Labs deep dive (2024, PDF)
source.page: Deep dive (November 2024), "What is Industrious Labs' cost-effectiveness?", pp. 14–16
source.quote: Our best guess is that Industrious Labs' aluminum corporate advocacy efforts avoid one tCO2 e for around $0.52 (range: $0.03-$12.30).

rows.explainer: Giving Green's best guess, which adds a small effect (a 0.1 percentage point higher chance, 10 years sooner) on half the global aluminium industry committing. Giving Green has "low confidence" in the analysis and says it "should not be taken literally"; its range is $0.03 to $12.30. The evaluator's own subjective guess, filed as a judgment.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂e averted through the automaker's own operations
rows.explainer: The campaign cost divided by Giving Green's cost per tonne for this narrowest case.

rows.label: Further tonnes through the rest of the car industry
Further tonnes through the wider aluminium industry
rows.explainer: Most of Giving Green's best guess comes from this step: two thirds of the tonnes. At the expensive end of Giving Green's range ($12.30) this row goes negative: the whole estimate is then smaller than the automaker-only case.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂e averted by the campaign
Cost per tonne of CO₂e averted
rows.explainer: Giving Green's bottom line: about 52 cents a tonne. Giving Green's research process page sets roughly $1 a tonne as the benchmark for a top climate nonprofit (https://www.givinggreen.earth/research/giving-greens-research-process).

rows.label: Years from the grant until the tonnes are avoided
rows.explainer: The campaign runs over several years from about 2022; carmakers' low-carbon aluminium purchases ramp up toward 2030, and two thirds of Giving Green's tonnes come from the wider aluminium industry committing ten years sooner, later still. Best guess 8 years from the money to the average tonne, 4 to 15. Our judgment. Giving Green counts a tonne the same whenever it is avoided; the site discounts every future benefit at the discount rate under Your values, in both views (an evaluator stating dollars per tonne takes no view on discounting). The heat deaths a tonne avoids are discounted again from the year it is avoided, in the site's climate conversion.

rows.label: A marginal dollar's tonnes as a share of the past average (our judgment)
rows.explainer: Our judgment, one figure for every model built on an organisation's past average (facts: meta.marginal_vs_past_average, shared with The Life You Can Save's leverage ratio): the cost per tonne is the cost of one past corporate campaign over its effect, an average; the next dollar does less than the average dollar did, since an organisation pursues its best opportunities first. 50%, from 18% to 100% (average = marginal). The evaluator view keeps 100%.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂e averted per dollar
rows.explainer: One over Giving Green's cost per tonne, discounted for the wait until the tonnes are avoided, like every future benefit on the site. How much air pollution these tonnes cut is the rows below. A marginal dollar is counted at the shared share of the past average (row above).

rows.label: Share of these tonnes from burning less fuel (smelter electricity)

source.title: ING Think, Greening aluminium: its less than shiny net zero reputation (2023)
source.note: Indirect emissions from power use are about 62% of the aluminium sector's emissions; about half of smelter electricity came from coal in 2021.

rows.explainer: Low-carbon aluminium cuts emissions mainly by running smelters on clean power instead of fossil power, and power is about 62% of the sector's emissions; the rest is anodes, alumina refining and process emissions. The high end adds the fuel burned for heat at alumina refineries; the low end allows for the cut coming more from inert anodes and recycling, which burn nothing less.

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths per tonne cut at North American smelters, relative to the fossil-fuel average

source.title: CATF, The Toll from Coal (2010), via Founders Pledge's CATF model; Markandya & Wilkinson (2007)
source.note: US coal plants after scrubbers: about 7.1 deaths per TWh at 0.82 t CO₂ per MWh (0.06 of the average); gas about 2.8 per TWh at 0.49 (0.04).

rows.explainer: The automaker's US production and the car industry's purchases (the first two steps) cut emissions at North American and imported-metal smelters, which run partly on hydro and partly on US coal and Gulf gas: about US coal's 0.06 of the average. Low 0.02: mostly gas and hydro. High 0.13: the Clean Air Task Force model's figure for US coal switched to gas.

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths per tonne cut across the global aluminium industry, relative to the fossil-fuel average

source.title: GBD MAPS Working Group (2016), Burden of disease attributable to coal-burning and other major sources of air pollution in China, HEI Special Report 20
source.quote: or coal combustion in power plants (86,500 deaths)
source.note: Deaths in 2013 from ambient PM2.5 due to coal burned in China's power plants. Divisor: China's coal-fired generation in 2013, 3,980,520 GWh (China Electricity Council, 2013 detailed electricity statistics, row 燃煤 (coal-fired) under 发电量 (generation), column 2013年; English mirror https://chinaenergyportal.org/en/2013-detailed-electricity-statistics/). Emission factor 0.82 t CO2 per MWh as in Founders Pledge's CATF model (IPCC AR5).

rows.explainer: Half the global aluminium industry (the third step, two thirds of the tonnes) is mostly Chinese smelters on coal power. China's power-plant coal caused about 86,500 deaths in 2013 (GBD MAPS 2016) over 3,981 TWh of coal-fired generation (China Electricity Council): about 21.7 deaths per TWh, close to Europe's 24.5, or 0.27 per 10,000 tonnes of CO₂ at 0.82 t per MWh, 0.18 of the world fossil-fuel average. Low 0.1: China's ultra-low-emission retrofits since 2014 have cut power-plant smoke. High 0.35: the extra smelter power coming from older plants upwind of cities, and the uncertainty in GBD MAPS's source attribution.

source.quote: If it additionally impacts the global automotive industry, cost-effectiveness improves to $1.50 per tCO2 e avoided.

rows.explainer: From Giving Green's figures: 1 − $0.52 ÷ $1.50, the share of its best guess's tonnes that come from the third step. Held at the best guess rather than computed from the cost rows, so the smoke mix doesn't swing with Giving Green's cost range (computing it there breaks the uncertainty split, since the same input would then drive both tonnes and smoke). The evaluator's own subjective guess, filed as a judgment.

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths per tonne of CO₂ cut, relative to the fossil-fuel average (tonne-weighted)
rows.explainer: The two regional figures above, weighted by where Giving Green's tonnes come from.

rows.label: Air pollution these tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne
rows.explainer: The row the site's climate conversion reads (docs/normalization.md 2.5): the air-pollution deaths each of these tonnes avoids, as a multiple of the world average behind the shared rate, 1.46 air-pollution deaths per 10,000 tonnes of CO₂ from fossil fuels (Rethink Priorities). The conversion values every tonne for its heat deaths (discounted over the decades until they come) and adds "Deaths caused by one more tonne of CO₂"'s air-pollution part times this row, at once. Here: the share of tonnes from smelter power times the smoke per tonne where those smelters are.

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths averted per tonne, counted directly by the evaluator (none here)
rows.explainer: A row every climate model has, which the site's conversion reads (docs/normalization.md 2.5): air-pollution deaths the evaluator counts itself, per tonne, on top of what the tonnes carry through air_pollution_weight. The evaluator counts none for this charity, so 0.

rows.label: Staff pay as a share of program cost
rows.explainer: Default for research, technical assistance and policy work: mostly people. Our judgment; we haven't seen this charity's breakdown.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable jobs elsewhere
rows.explainer: Researchers, lawyers and advocates could typically earn considerably more in consulting, law firms or industry. Our judgment.

rows.label: Salary forgone by staff per dollar of cost (in-kind donation)
Share of the full cost paid in cash
rows.explainer: With credit by share of resources, staff's forgone pay counts as part of the cost, and staff get their share of the outcome. Off, this is 100%.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂e averted per dollar donated
rows.explainer: The figure per dollar above; with credit by share of resources, times the share of the full cost paid in cash (staff's forgone pay is the rest). The site turns these tonnes into years of healthy life through the deaths they avoid: "Deaths caused by one more tonne of CO₂", its heat part discounted over "Years until the heat deaths from a tonne of CO₂" for every tonne, and its air-pollution part, at once, times "Air pollution these tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne" above.
